newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors ask acquittal of arson suspect.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors ask acquittal of arson suspect.

text.p: German prosecutors on Wednesday took the unusual step of demanding an acquittal for a Lebanese man charged with starting a fire that killed 10 people, saying there was not enough evidence to convict him.

"The trial has not produced enough evidence to convict him," state prosecutor Michael Boeckenhauer told the court. "Therefore the accused must be acquitted, even if that judgement wouldn't fit with the final truth."

The Lebanese man, Safwan Eid, has been on trial since last September on charges of aggravated arson and causing bodily harm after a fire at a refugee hostel in January 1996 in which 10 people died and 38 were injured.
Eid, who also lived in the hostel, has denied all charges. The defence still has to sum up its case before the judge delivers a final judgement.

The fire was the worst disaster to hit a hostel for refugees in Germany, and at first raised fears of a new wave of neo-Nazi racist violence similar to one which swept across the country after unification in 1990.
But police arrested Eid, a civil war refugee who lived in the hostel with his family for six years, on suspicion of trying to get revenge in a petty quarrel with another resident.
The fire killed six people from Zaire, a man from Benin, a Lebanese and a woman from Angola and her six-year-old daughter.

Boeckenhauer said that despite the testimony of around 100 witnesses there was no exact information about how the fire started, although it was clear that the blaze had broken out on the first floor of the hostel.
Eid's defence team say the fire started on the ground floor near the entrance, suggesting an attack from outside.
Boeckenhauer said it was no longer certain beyond doubt that Eid had, as charged, poured flammable liquid in front of a door and set fire to it to take revenge on a fellow refugee.
Eid's defence claims right-wing extremists from the eastern town of Mecklenburg were behind the attack.
Prosecutors had based their case on three words Eid allegedly told a first aid worker after he was rescued: "It was us."
Eid, however, told the court that what he really said was: "It was them -- they set the stairs on fire," repeating something his father had just told him.
Asked by one of his defence team what his father had meant, Safwan Eid said: "It was obvious that when he said they he was talking about the Nazis."
Anti-racist and left-wing groups say the fire was a neo-Nazi attack and the accused was a victim.
Eid's defence team argue that prosecutors did not properly investigate four youths, including a skinhead from a local far-right group, who were detained near the scene.
Three of the young men, driving a stolen car, had singed hair. But police accepted their alibis and released them.
